questoes.pergunta: An HR software company extracts fields from customers' employment contracts into its payroll product. Extractions whose fields all score above a calibrated 0.92 confidence threshold are posted to payroll automatically; the rest go to a review queue, and the monitoring dashboard computes the error rate from reviewer corrections. For five months the dashboard showed a stable 1.2% error rate. Then a customer audit found that 18% of auto-posted probation end dates had been wrong since a large client adopted a new contract template, all with confidence of at least 0.95. What is the most likely reason this went undetected?
opcoes: The 0.92 threshold was calibrated on a labeled set that was too small for date fields, so it should have been set higher for them from the start.
The extraction prompt had no few-shot examples of the new template, so the model could not handle the changed position of the probation clause.
The dashboard averaged the error rate across all customers instead of reporting it per customer account, which diluted the large client's errors.
Error rates were measured only on extractions sent to reviewers; no random sample of the auto-posted, high-confidence ones was ever checked.
questoes.explicacao: The dashboard only saw extractions that reviewers touched, which are the low-confidence ones, so errors in the auto-posted set were invisible by construction. Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions (by document type, field, and template), reviewed by people, measures their ongoing error rate and surfaces novel error patterns such as a new contract template. Without it, a confidently wrong segment can run for months.
feedbacks: Calibration quality matters, but the errors started when a new template appeared after calibration; a higher threshold set once would not have revealed them. The gap is that nobody measured the auto-posted set over time.
This may explain why the dates were wrong, but the question is why the problem went undetected for five months. Missing few-shot examples do not explain a monitoring blind spot.
Splitting the same data per customer would still include only reviewer-corrected extractions. The auto-posted ones were never in the data, so segmenting it would not have shown the errors.
Correct. Only a random sample of the auto-approved, high-confidence extractions measures their real error rate and catches novel error patterns such as a changed template.

questoes.pergunta: A health insurer uses a multi-agent research system to produce a quarterly brief on specialty drug spending. Subagents return quarterly cost figures per drug class from financial filings, recent news coverage of pricing policy, and technical findings from clinical studies. The report subagent's prompt says: "Convert every finding into a bullet of at most 25 words so that all sections look consistent." Reviewers say the cost comparison across 9 drug classes and 6 quarters is hard to follow and the pricing news reads as disconnected fragments. What is the flaw in this implementation?
opcoes: The bullets lack worked examples; few-shot examples of well-written bullets would make each cost and news item more informative to reviewers.
It forces one format on all content; cost figures should be rendered as a table, news as prose, and the study findings as a structured list.
The bullets carry no claim-source mappings, so reviewers cannot trace each figure or headline back to the filing or article it came from.
The brief carries too many raw figures; synthesis should report average quarter-over-quarter change per class to keep each bullet short.
questoes.explicacao: The complaints come from the uniform format: a 9-by-6 cost comparison is a table, news needs connected prose for context, and study results fit a structured list. Synthesis outputs should render each content type appropriately rather than converting everything into one format. The other options address real concerns, but not the readability problem described.
feedbacks: Better-written bullets still scatter a 54-cell comparison across bullets and chop the news into fragments. Few-shot examples improve consistency within a format; they do not fix choosing the wrong format.
Correct. Financial data reads best as a table, news as prose, and technical findings as a structured list; forcing every finding into uniform bullets causes exactly these complaints.
Claim-source mappings matter for provenance, but reviewers did not complain about traceability. They complained about readability, which comes from the forced format.
Averaging discards the per-quarter figures reviewers need to compare and still leaves the news as fragments. It treats a rendering problem by losing data.

questoes.pergunta: A health insurer's research system studies outcomes of remote monitoring for heart-failure patients. The web search and document analysis subagents each return a few paragraphs summarizing what they read. In a 42-claim report, compliance reviewers find that 11 claims cite the wrong study or no study, although every one of those claims appears in at least one source the subagents read. Checked one by one, the subagent summaries are accurate. Which statement about this behavior is correct?
opcoes: The synthesis subagent is producing unsupported claims, so it needs a verify_fact tool to confirm each statement on the web before the report goes out.
Attribution was lost when the findings were compressed into prose; subagents should return each claim with its source URL, document name, and excerpt.
The synthesis subagent receives too much text, so the coordinator should pass it only the highest-ranked summaries to keep its citations accurate.
The citations are unstable between runs, so the system should run synthesis twice and keep only citations that both runs attach to the same claim.
questoes.explicacao: The claims are true and the summaries accurate, so the facts survived; what was lost is which source supports which claim. When findings are compressed into prose, claim-source mappings disappear. Having subagents emit structured mappings (source URL, document name, relevant excerpt) that synthesis preserves fixes attribution at its root.
feedbacks: The claims are supported by sources the subagents read, so they are not hallucinated. A verification tool re-finds facts but does not restore which source each claim came from.
Correct. Prose summaries drop the link between claim and source; structured claim-source mappings let the synthesis keep attribution intact.
Trimming input can help when context is overloaded, but the issue is that attribution was never passed in a structured form. Fewer summaries would also drop valid findings.
Voting between runs only keeps citations that are consistently guessed. If the mapping was never passed, both runs can agree on the wrong source.

questoes.pergunta: An HR software company extracts data from onboarding packets: offer letters, tax withholding forms, direct-deposit forms, and emergency-contact forms, in four languages. After three months in which a person reviewed every extraction, accuracy on extractions above 0.9 confidence is 98.6%, above the 97% target set by the payroll team. The product manager proposes turning off human review for all extractions above 0.9 starting next sprint. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Hold it until accuracy is broken down by document type, field, and language, then automate only the segments that meet the target on their own.
Approve it, since three months of full review is a large labeled sample and 98.6% clears the payroll team's 97% target by a safe margin.
Hold it until a uniform 2% random sample of production documents confirms the 98.6% figure over one more full month of live traffic.
Approve it first for the highest-volume document types, since they dominate the 98.6% figure and account for most of the review cost.
questoes.explicacao: A 98.6% aggregate can hide a document type, field, or language that performs far worse, because high-volume segments dominate the average. Before automating high-confidence extractions, validate accuracy per segment and automate only the segments that meet the target independently. The three months of reviewed data already make that breakdown possible.
feedbacks: Correct. Segmenting by document type and field (and here, language) shows whether performance is consistent before review is removed.
The sample is large, but it is summarized as one number. A weak segment, such as one language or one form, can sit well below 97% while the aggregate looks safe.
Another month of a uniform sample re-measures the same aggregate; a weak document type or field stays hidden inside 98.6% however long you wait.
Volume is not a readiness criterion. A high-volume type may still have a weak field, and the decision should rest on each segment's measured accuracy.

questoes.pergunta: An HR software company extracts pay figures from about 300 published salary surveys and compensation reports to build a benchmark report for its customers. For some roles the surveys agree; for others they diverge, and some surveys describe their own figures as "preliminary" or "base pay only, n=48". Today the report shows one median per role, with all source names in a footnote. Several customers made offers based on figures that turned out to be disputed among the surveys. Which TWO changes best address this? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Rewrite every survey's description of its figures into one standard phrase, so that customers are not confused by each survey's own terminology.
Split each role's results into a well-established section where surveys agree and a contested section listing the diverging figures with their sources.
Compute a single figure per role as a median weighted by each survey's sample size, so that the largest and most robust surveys drive the value customers see.
Keep only the figures from the three most-cited surveys for each role, so the report shows one consistent value that customers can rely on.
Show each survey's own qualifiers and method notes, such as "preliminary" or "base pay only, n=48", right next to the figures they describe.
questoes.explicacao: Customers need to see which figures are consensus and which are disputed, so the report should separate well-established from contested findings, with each diverging value tied to its source. It should also preserve each source's own characterizations and methodological context, because "preliminary" or "base pay only" changes how a figure should be used. Collapsing to one value or normalizing the wording removes exactly that information.
feedbacks: Normalizing the wording strips the original characterizations, such as "preliminary", that tell customers how much weight a figure can bear.
Correct. Explicit well-established and contested sections let customers see which figures are disputed and by which sources.
A weighted median is still one number that no survey published, and it hides that the surveys disagree. It also discards each survey's qualifiers.
Dropping surveys hides the disagreement instead of reporting it, so customers would again treat a disputed figure as settled.
Correct. Preserving each source's qualifiers and method notes keeps the context needed to judge and compare figures.

questoes.pergunta: A health insurer's research system is evaluating a home-nursing program. The document analysis subagent reviews 14 studies, and two credible studies of comparable populations report 30-day readmission reductions of 12% and 21%. Today, when the subagent detects a conflict like this, it stops and returns only "conflicting data found" to the coordinator, so the remaining 9 studies are never analyzed and the run ends without a report. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Have the subagent keep the value from the study with the larger sample, note the other one in a footnote, and continue with the remaining studies.
Have the subagent send both conflicting studies straight to the synthesis subagent, which already compares sources while drafting the report.
Have the subagent pause and ask the user which study to trust, then resume the remaining studies once the user has answered the question.
Have the subagent finish all 14 studies with both values included and annotated, and let the coordinator decide how to reconcile them.
questoes.explicacao: The subagent should complete its analysis, including the conflicting values explicitly annotated with their sources, and hand the decision to the coordinator, which reconciles before passing anything to synthesis. That keeps the 9 unanalyzed studies in scope and puts reconciliation where the overall context is. Picking a value, bypassing the coordinator, or blocking on the user each lose either information or progress.
feedbacks: Choosing by sample size is an arbitrary resolution made by the wrong agent; both credible values should be reported with attribution so the conflict stays visible.
This bypasses the coordinator, which should decide how to reconcile before synthesis, and the synthesis agent may silently pick one value while writing.
Blocking the analysis on a user answer stalls the run; the subagent can finish its work and let the coordinator handle the conflict.
Correct. Finish the analysis with the conflicting values annotated, and let the coordinator decide how to reconcile before synthesis.

questoes.pergunta: A health insurer's research system has a document analysis subagent that downloads papers from a journal repository. On a run about biosimilar insulin switching, the repository returned 503 errors for 6 of 19 papers even after the subagent's own retries. The team is debating the subagent's return value. Design X returns {"status": "error", "message": "document analysis failed"} so the coordinator re-runs the delegation. Design Y returns the 13 completed analyses as a normal result and leaves out the 6 failures. Which approach best enables coordinator recovery?
opcoes: Design X, because an explicit failure status stops the coordinator from moving on to synthesis with an incomplete set of papers.
Design Y, because 13 of 19 papers is adequate coverage and it spares the coordinator from repeating the whole delegation.
Neither: return the 13 analyses with the failure type, the 6 paper IDs and retries attempted, and options like a preprint server.
Design X, with exponential backoff added in the coordinator, so the delegation is repeated until all 19 papers download successfully.
questoes.explicacao: The coordinator can only choose well (retry just the 6 later, try another source, or proceed and annotate the gap) if it knows what failed, what was tried, and what already succeeded. Design X throws away 13 good analyses behind a generic status; Design Y hides the failure as if the set were complete. Structured error context with partial results and alternatives enables intelligent recovery.
feedbacks: A generic failure discards the 13 completed analyses and gives the coordinator nothing to decide with; it can only repeat the whole task.
Silently dropping the 6 failures looks like success, so neither the coordinator nor the final report would know the coverage is incomplete.
Correct. Failure type, attempted items, partial results, and alternatives give the coordinator what it needs to recover intelligently.
Repeating the full delegation until everything succeeds wastes the completed work and may never finish if the repository stays down.

questoes.pergunta: An HR software company builds a benefits profile for each employee by merging three extraction passes: one over the benefits enrollment form, one over the plan summary PDF, and one over the payroll deduction report. Today the merge step outputs only the final value of each field. When the enrollment form lists 3 dependents and the deduction report implies 2, auditors cannot tell which document said what and must reopen all three files. Which TWO design choices best preserve provenance through the merge? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Have the merge step keep the value from the most recently dated document and drop the others, so the profile has no duplicate entries.
Have the merge step write a short narrative summary of each profile, so auditors read the context before checking values.
Have each extraction pass emit every value together with its source document ID, page number, and the exact excerpt it was read from.
Have the merge step combine entries for the same field into one that keeps all supporting sources and flags differing values.
Have each extraction pass attach a confidence score to every value, so the merge step can keep the highest-confidence value per field.
questoes.explicacao: Provenance survives only if each value carries its source mapping from the start and the merge step preserves and merges those mappings instead of collapsing them. Emitting document, page, and excerpt per value, then merging same-field entries while keeping every source and flagging disagreements, lets auditors see which document said what. Keeping one value, whether by recency or confidence, discards the other sources.
feedbacks: Keeping the most recent value arbitrarily resolves the disagreement and erases which document said what.
A narrative summary compresses the findings and loses the field-to-document links that auditors need.
Correct. Structured claim-source mappings at extraction time are what later steps need in order to preserve attribution.
Correct. Merging same-field entries while keeping all sources and flagging differences preserves the mappings through the merge.
Confidence can help route review, but keeping only the highest-confidence value still discards the other sources and hides the disagreement.

questoes.pergunta: An HR software company extracts fields from employee expense documents: hotel invoices, taxi receipts, meal receipts, and mileage logs. The monthly accuracy report, based on a labeled review sample, has shown 97.4% for six months. One customer's finance team nevertheless reports frequent errors in mileage reimbursements, which they check line by line. Mileage logs are about 3% of all documents processed. What is the most likely root cause of the gap between the reported metric and the customer's experience?
opcoes: The 97.4% figure is an aggregate across document types and fields; a small segment such as mileage logs can perform much worse without moving it.
The monthly review sample is too small to measure accuracy precisely, so the true overall rate is likely several points below the reported 97.4%.
The customer's finance team applies stricter matching rules than the labeled sample does, so it flags values as errors that the metric accepts.
The schema marks the distance field as required, so whenever a log omits it the model fabricates a value just to satisfy the schema.
questoes.explicacao: A 3% segment can have poor accuracy and barely move a 97.4% average, so the aggregate metric masks it. Reporting accuracy by document type and field would show the mileage-log segment directly. The other options describe possible issues but do not explain why a stable aggregate coexists with frequent errors in one document type.
feedbacks: Correct. Aggregate accuracy can hide poor performance on a specific document type or field; segment the metric to see it.
Sample size affects precision, but the customer's problem is concentrated in one document type, and even a perfectly precise aggregate would hide it.
Different matching rules could inflate the complaint, but nothing in the situation suggests it; the simpler explanation is a weak segment hidden by the average.
Required fields can cause fabrication, and that might be one source of the errors, but it does not explain why the monthly metric failed to reveal them.

questoes.pergunta: An online electronics retailer's support agent, built with the Claude Agent SDK, delegates warranty checks to a warranty subagent that calls manufacturer APIs. Whenever a manufacturer call fails, the subagent immediately returns {"error": "warranty check failed"} and the coordinator re-runs the whole warranty delegation. Logs show that 70% of these failures are brief 503 responses that succeed on a second call, and each full re-run adds about 40 seconds while the customer waits. What is the flaw in this implementation?
opcoes: The coordinator retries instead of escalating; it should hand the conversation to a human whenever the subagent reports any failure.
The subagent surfaces failures; it should return "no active warranty" on any API error so that the conversation keeps moving.
The subagent does not recover locally; it should retry transient errors itself and pass up only unresolved ones with what it tried.
The coordinator retries without backoff; it should wait with exponential backoff before each re-run so the API has time to recover.
questoes.explicacao: Most failures are transient and resolve on a second call, so the subagent should retry them locally and propagate only errors it cannot resolve, together with what it attempted and any partial results. Bubbling every 503 up makes the coordinator repeat the full delegation and multiplies latency. Escalating every failure, suppressing failures, or centralizing retries in the coordinator each create a different problem.
feedbacks: Escalating every failure pushes recoverable, transient errors onto human agents and hurts first-contact resolution.
Returning "no active warranty" on an API error is silent suppression: the customer is told something false about their warranty.
Correct. Local recovery for transient failures, propagating only unresolved errors with attempts and partial results, removes the full re-runs.
Backoff in the coordinator still repeats the whole delegation for errors the subagent could have retried cheaply, and it adds waiting time.

questoes.pergunta: A health insurer's research system reports on type 2 diabetes prevalence among members aged 40 to 64. A recent report labeled two sources as contradictory: a national survey giving 11.3% and a state registry giving 14.8%. An analyst found that the survey data were collected in 2019 and the registry data in 2025, but neither date appeared in the subagents' outputs. Similar false conflicts appear in 6 of the last 22 reports. Which TWO changes best address this? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Have the synthesis compare values only within the same collection period and present values from different periods as a trend.
Instruct the synthesis subagent to prefer the most recently published source whenever two credible values for the same measure differ.
Have the coordinator drop sources older than five years before delegating, so synthesis compares current data only.
Have the synthesis average differing values from credible sources and show the full range in a footnote, so readers see both.
Require the search and analysis subagents to output each statistic with its publication date and its data collection period.
questoes.explicacao: The conflict was an artifact of missing dates: values from 2019 and 2025 describe different periods, not a contradiction. Subagents must include publication and data collection dates in their structured outputs, and the synthesis must use those dates to interpret values over time. Preferring recent sources, dropping older ones, or averaging all discard or distort real information.
feedbacks: Correct. Using the dates to compare like with like turns false contradictions into the time series they actually are.
Preferring recency arbitrarily picks one value and would also hide genuine conflicts between sources from the same period.
Dropping older sources removes valid data, such as the baseline of a trend, instead of interpreting it correctly.
Averaging values from different years produces a figure no source reported and still treats a temporal difference as a conflict.
Correct. Publication and collection dates in the structured output are what make correct temporal interpretation possible.

questoes.pergunta: An airline's platform team built an Agent SDK tool that, before a library upgrade, maps every call site of a deprecated booking-API client across 38 internal repositories, using one subagent per group of repositories. Today, if any subagent fails, for example on a repository it lacks permission to clone, the coordinator raises an exception and the whole 25-minute run is lost. A teammate proposes wrapping each subagent in a try/catch that returns an empty call-site list on failure, so the run always completes. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Accept it, since an unreadable repository has no call sites the agent could change anyway, so an empty list is accurate for planning.
Reject it; report each failed repository with the failure and what was attempted, and let the run finish for the other repositories.
Accept it if each caught failure is logged to a file, so that engineers can check the log for any gaps before they merge the upgrade.
Reject it and keep the current behavior, since an upgrade plan with any missing repository is unreliable and must be rerun in full.
questoes.explicacao: Both the current behavior and the proposal are anti-patterns: aborting the whole run discards the work done on every other repository, while returning an empty list presents a failure as "no call sites". The run should continue for the repositories that succeeded and report each failure with its type and what was attempted, so the coordinator and the plan show the gap explicitly.
feedbacks: An empty list claims the repository has no call sites when the agent never read it; the upgrade would then break code nobody analyzed.
Correct. Neither suppress nor abort: continue with the successful repositories and propagate each failure with its context.
Logging moves the burden to engineers who must remember to check a file, while the plan itself still reports the failure as "no call sites".
Terminating on a single failure throws away every successful analysis; a plan with an explicit, annotated gap is more useful than no plan.

questoes.pergunta: An online electronics retailer's support coordinator delegates order-history lookups to an order subagent that queries two backends: the current order service and a legacy archive for orders older than 18 months. The archive often times out. When it does, the subagent returns {"status": "failed"}, even though it already has the customer's recent orders, and the coordinator tells the customer it cannot access their orders; 23% of those conversations then escalate. The archive cannot be changed this quarter. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Have the coordinator transfer the conversation to a human whenever the order subagent reports a failure, since the archive is unreliable.
Remove the archive query from the subagent, so it relies on the current order service and stops reporting failures to the coordinator.
Raise the subagent's archive timeout from 8 to 30 seconds, so that more archive queries finish before the subagent gives up on them.
Have the subagent return the recent orders plus the failure type, the archive query attempted, and options such as retrying later.
questoes.explicacao: With structured context (failure type, attempted query, partial results, and alternatives), the coordinator can answer from the recent orders it already has and decide how to handle questions about older ones. That turns an all-or-nothing failure into an informed recovery decision without changing the archive.
feedbacks: Escalating every failure sends cases the agent could resolve with recent orders to humans, which lowers first-contact resolution.
Silently dropping the archive means older orders appear not to exist, so customers asking about them would get wrong answers.
A longer timeout makes customers wait and still fails when the archive is down; it does not change the all-or-nothing result.
Correct. Structured error context with partial results lets the coordinator answer from recent orders and decide how to handle the archive gap.

questoes.pergunta: An HR software company extracts headcount and turnover figures from companies' annual reports and regulatory filings for a benchmarking product. A validation step sets conflict_detected to true when two documents for the same company give different headcounts. Now 31% of companies are flagged, and analysts find that most flags compare a 2023 annual report with a 2025 filing. The extraction schema has no date fields. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Add fields for each figure's publication date and the period it refers to, so validation compares values only within the same period.
Have validation keep the larger headcount when two values differ by less than 15%, so that small differences stop raising conflict flags.
Route every flagged company to an analyst for review, since a person should decide which headcount is correct before benchmarking.
Add few-shot examples that show the model how to pick the more reliable document when two headcount figures for a company differ.
questoes.explicacao: Most flags are temporal differences, not contradictions: a 2023 and a 2025 headcount are expected to differ. Capturing publication date and reference period in the structured output lets validation compare like with like while true conflicts stay flagged. Tolerance thresholds, mass human review, or picking a document treat the symptom without the missing data.
feedbacks: Correct. Dates in the structured output prevent temporal differences from being misread as contradictions.
A tolerance threshold hides real conflicts below 15% and still flags genuine growth above it; it ignores the information that explains the flags.
Sending 31% of companies to analysts overloads reviewers with cases that are mostly not conflicts at all.
Picking one document arbitrarily resolves what is mostly a time difference, and it would also hide real conflicts.

questoes.pergunta: An airline's developer productivity agent writes a dossier on the legacy crew-scheduling service by combining code analysis with Grep and Read, the internal wiki through one MCP server, and incident tickets through another. During one run the wiki server was unreachable for the whole session, so the architecture and runbook sections were written from code alone. Design X holds the dossier until every source is available. Design Y publishes it as usual. Which approach should the team adopt?
opcoes: Design X, since a dossier written without the wiki could mislead on-call engineers, so it should wait until every source responds.
Design Y, with a general notice at the top saying the dossier may be incomplete and that readers should verify important details.
Design Y, with coverage annotations stating which sections are well supported and which have gaps because the wiki was down.
Design Y, with the agent filling the missing runbook steps from the dossiers of similar services and clearly marking them as inferred.
questoes.explicacao: A dossier is still valuable when one source is down, as long as readers know where it is solid and where it is not. Coverage annotations mark well-supported findings versus topic areas with gaps due to unavailable sources, which a generic disclaimer cannot do. Blocking the output or filling gaps from other systems are both worse.
feedbacks: Blocking the dossier until every source is up is the terminate-on-single-failure pattern; most of the content is valid and useful now.
A generic notice does not say which sections lack support, so readers cannot tell the architecture gap from the solid incident history.
Correct. Coverage annotations distinguish well-supported sections from gaps caused by the unavailable wiki.
Borrowing runbook steps from other services fills the gap with content that may not apply here; the gap itself should be stated.

questoes.pergunta: An HR software company's compliance team sets a requirement: human review of extracted onboarding data may be reduced only where extraction is reliable for every field that feeds payroll. The current plan uses a weekly report of overall accuracy on reviewed samples (98.1% last week) and cuts review to 10% of documents once that figure stays above 98% for four consecutive weeks. What should you change to meet the requirement?
opcoes: Raise the weekly bar from 98% to 99.5% and extend the stability window to eight weeks before review is reduced anywhere.
Report accuracy per document type and per payroll field, and reduce review only for segments that meet the target on their own.
Replace the weekly figure with a rolling 30-day average, so that short dips in accuracy cannot trigger a premature reduction.
Attach a document-level confidence score and reduce review only for documents whose score is above 0.95 on the review sample.
questoes.explicacao: The requirement is per field, but the plan measures one overall number, which can stay above 98% while a payroll field fails. Breaking accuracy down by document type and field, and reducing review only where each segment meets the target, satisfies the requirement directly. Stricter or smoother aggregates are still aggregates.
feedbacks: A higher aggregate bar is still a single number; one payroll field can be failing while the overall figure exceeds 99.5%.
Correct. Per-document-type and per-field accuracy verifies consistent performance across segments before review is reduced.
Smoothing changes timing, not granularity; a weak field stays hidden inside the rolling average.
A document-level score blends strong and weak fields together, so it cannot show that every payroll field is reliable.

questoes.pergunta: A health insurer's research system compiles coverage policies for continuous glucose monitors across 12 state Medicaid programs. The report states "no published coverage policy found" for 4 states, but a policy analyst finds published policies for 3 of them. Logs show that the document analysis subagent's portal requests for those 3 states ran for 30 seconds and ended without a response, while the request for the 4th state returned HTTP 200 with an empty list. The subagent's output was identical for all four states. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: The synthesis subagent lacks explicit instructions to double-check negative findings, so it reported missing policies without questioning them.
The coordinator assigned all 12 states to a single subagent instead of splitting them, so that subagent ran out of time on some states.
The subagent's portal searches used terms that were too narrow, so the 3 published policies did not match its search keywords.
The subagent reported failed requests the same way as searches with no matches, so each lookup failure read as "no policy exists".
questoes.explicacao: Three lookups never completed, yet the subagent reported them exactly like the one search that genuinely found nothing. Access failures need retry or recovery decisions, while valid empty results are findings; conflating them turned failures into false negatives. The subagent should report the timeouts as structured errors so the coordinator can retry or annotate the gap.
feedbacks: Double-checking at synthesis treats the symptom; the synthesis had no way to know which empty results were failures because the subagent made them identical.
Decomposition can matter at scale, but the logs show the portal requests themselves timed out, not that the subagent ran out of time on its task.
Narrow search terms would yield an HTTP 200 with no matches; these requests never got a response at all.
Correct. Distinguishing access failures from valid empty results lets the coordinator retry or flag the 3 states instead of reporting false negatives.

questoes.pergunta: An HR software company extracts data from about 4,000 employment-verification letters a day; three reviewers can check about 350. The model outputs field-level confidence scores, and thresholds were calibrated on a labeled validation set. Extractions are queued for review in arrival order; reviewers work from the top until the day ends, and whatever is left is posted automatically. Letters whose header and body state different job titles or salaries are handled like any other letter. What is the flaw in this workflow?
opcoes: The thresholds come from a set labeled only once; calibration should be redone every day on the latest letters before the queue is built.
Letters should not be posted without review at all; every letter should wait in the queue until a reviewer is able to check it.
Reviewer time goes by arrival order; low-confidence fields and letters with contradictory content should be routed and reviewed first.
Reviewers should check a uniform random 350 letters each day instead, so that the accuracy they measure is unbiased across all letters.
questoes.explicacao: With limited reviewer capacity, the queue must be prioritized: route extractions with low calibrated confidence and documents with ambiguous or contradictory content to review first, and let the rest post. Arrival order spends reviewers on easy letters while risky ones post unchecked. Random sampling of the auto-posted set still has a role, but for measuring error rates, not for routing the day's risky cases.
feedbacks: Daily recalibration is heavy and does not change the core problem: the queue ignores which letters are risky.
Holding every letter for review ignores the 350-per-day capacity; the backlog would grow by thousands of letters each day.
Correct. Route low-confidence and contradictory extractions to people first, so limited reviewer capacity goes where errors are likely.
A uniform sample measures accuracy, but as a routing policy it sends mostly easy letters to reviewers and lets the risky ones post.

questoes.pergunta: A health insurer's research system asks its document analysis subagent to analyze 8 payer policy PDFs on gene therapy coverage. The subagent returns {"status": "source unavailable"}. Its logs show 5 PDFs analyzed successfully, 2 behind a login page, and 1 that timed out twice. The coordinator re-delegated the whole task three times, each failing the same way, and then reported that the analysis was unavailable. Which statement about this behavior is correct?
opcoes: The generic status hid what failed, so the coordinator could not keep the 5 analyses, skip the 2 login-gated PDFs, and retry only the timeout.
The coordinator retried too few times; with a longer backoff schedule, the login-gated PDFs would likely have opened on a later attempt.
The subagent should have retried the 2 login-gated PDFs locally with backoff before reporting, since local recovery would resolve them.
The coordinator behaved correctly, since a source-unavailable status means the subagent's entire task has to be treated as failed.
questoes.explicacao: A single "source unavailable" status collapsed three different situations: 5 successes, 2 permission failures that retries cannot fix, and 1 transient timeout worth retrying. Without that context the coordinator could only repeat the whole task. Structured error context would have let it keep the partial results, skip futile retries, and retry only the timeout.
feedbacks: Correct. Generic error statuses hide the information the coordinator needs to choose a targeted recovery.
Login-gated documents are a permission problem; more retries with longer backoff would fail the same way and waste time.
Local recovery is right for transient failures, but a login page is not transient, so retrying it locally would not resolve it.
Treating the whole task as failed discards 5 good analyses; the status should have described what failed and what succeeded.

questoes.pergunta: An HR software company extracts 22 fields from employment contracts, and the model outputs a confidence score for each field. An engineer proposes routing any contract with a field below 0.85 to human review, using the same threshold for every field, because the scores looked reasonable on 30 contracts he checked by hand. The team also has 1,200 contracts that reviewers labeled last quarter. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Keep the per-field scores, but set each field's threshold from the 1,200 labeled contracts by checking accuracy at each score level.
Accept it as proposed, since one shared threshold is easier for reviewers to understand and the hand check showed sensible scores.
Replace the per-field scores with one contract-level score averaged over the 22 fields, so routing relies on a single stable number.
Drop confidence-based routing and send a uniform 15% random sample of contracts to review, since model scores cannot be trusted.
questoes.explicacao: Field-level confidence is a valid routing signal once it is calibrated: use the labeled validation set to see how accuracy varies with the score for each field, and set per-field thresholds that meet the error target. A single threshold validated on 30 contracts is uncalibrated, averaging hides weak fields, and abandoning confidence routing throws away a useful signal.
feedbacks: Correct. Calibrating per-field thresholds on a labeled validation set turns the model's scores into a reliable routing signal.
Thirty hand-checked contracts cannot show how accuracy varies with the score for each of 22 fields, and fields differ in how well their scores track accuracy.
Averaging across fields hides a weak field behind strong ones, which is exactly what field-level scores are meant to expose.
Raw scores need calibration, but calibrated field-level confidence is the recommended routing signal; a uniform sample spends reviewer time on easy contracts.
